name: Thematic Coding
title: Thematic Coding
answer: Thematic coding is a qualitative method for finding, naming, and organizing patterns of meaning across a body of text, audio, image, or video data. It is used in interview studies, focus groups, open-ended survey responses, field notes, documents, and case records. The approach can be inductive, where themes emerge from the data, or deductive, where themes come from an existing framework or theory. It also supports mixed methods designs by turning coded segments into categories that can be compared with quantitative results. It is distinct from topic modeling, which is a computational text-mining technique, though the two are sometimes used together.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Thematic coding is a qualitative method for finding, naming, and organizing patterns of meaning across a body of text, audio, image, or video data. It is used in interview studies, focus groups, open-ended survey responses, field notes, documents, and case records. The approach can be inductive, where themes emerge from the data, or deductive, where themes come from an existing framework or theory. It also supports mixed methods designs by turning coded segments into categories that can be compared with quantitative results. It is distinct from topic modeling, which is a computational text-mining technique, though the two are sometimes used together.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a corpus of source material, a coding frame or codebook, and a system for storing and retrieving coded segments. Many teams use qualitative data analysis software such as NVivo, MAXQDA, or ATLAS.ti to manage transcripts, audio, and annotations. Others work with spreadsheets, word processors, or shared documents when the corpus is small. The infrastructure also includes version control for the codebook, secure storage for participant data, and a clear file naming convention. In AI-assisted workflows, a language model may suggest codes or cluster passages, but the human coder remains responsible for the final scheme.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The analyst reads the data closely, marks segments that carry meaning, and assigns codes that describe what the segment is about. Codes are then compared, merged, split, or grouped into candidate themes, and the analyst writes definitions and boundary rules for each theme. The process is iterative, moving back and forth between the data, the codebook, and the emerging themes until the scheme is stable. Teams often test reliability by having two or more coders code the same sample and then discuss disagreements. The final output is a narrative account of themes supported by quoted evidence and a transparent account of decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Thematic coding handles human subjects data, so consent, confidentiality, and data protection rules apply from collection through storage and publication. Provenance matters because a theme should be traceable to the coded segments and the original source, not just to an analyst's summary. When AI tools are used to suggest codes or summarize passages, the team should record which tool, which version, and which prompts or settings were used, and keep the raw model output separate from human decisions. Copyright and licensing also apply to documents, transcripts, and media that are coded. The audit trail, including code definitions, memos, and changes to the codebook, is part of the evidence that the analysis is trustworthy.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Thematic coding is increasingly combined with computational methods, including natural language processing and large language models, to help with initial coding, code suggestion, and theme exploration at scale. At the same time, qualitative researchers are pushing back on full automation, arguing that interpretation, context, and reflexivity cannot be delegated to a model. Expect more hybrid workflows where AI handles sorting and pattern detection while humans own the conceptual work and the final account. Standards for reporting AI-assisted qualitative analysis are still forming, and journals and ethics boards are likely to ask for more detail about model use. The method itself remains recognizable, a disciplined way to turn messy human material into defensible themes.
